newsitem.title: ITALY: CLOCK TICKING FOR ITALY IN EMU RACE AGAINST TIME.
newsitem.headline: CLOCK TICKING FOR ITALY IN EMU RACE AGAINST TIME.

text.p: Prime Minister Romano Prodi has staked his political future on a forthcoming mini-budget and will fight to ensure Italy is ready for the birth of the single European currency, politicians and commentators said on Tuesday.
His centre-left government faces stiff opposition from its Communist Refoundation parliamentary ally over much-needed spending adjustments -- but time is running out.

"There is no alternative to this government...we have to get our accounts in order now. In the end I think we will strike a compromise deal," said Enrico Letta, deputy leader of the Popular Party (PPI), a centrist group in Prodi's coalition.

Treasury Minister Carlo Azeglio Ciampi has said Italy needs to save around 14 trillion lire ($8.3 billion) this year to make the grade for European economic and monetary union (EMU) and is busy working on a package of deficit-cutting measures.
"I think there is the growing realisation that no one can gain any political or economic advantage from Italy missing EMU," Letta told Reuters in an interview.

On paper Italy is still far from reaching some of the goals laid down in the Maastricht Treaty for EMU aspirants, with the state deficit at 6.8 percent of gross domestic product in 1996 against a target of three percent.
But it is fighting hard to cut this differential with a huge 62.5 trillion lire budget introduced at the end of last year and fresh budgetary rigour in the offing.
Prodi knows that many Germans do not want Italy, with its recent history of lira devaluations and political instability, to be in at the start of EMU.
But domestic concerns count for more than German worries and Prodi has pledged to resign if he fails to make the EMU grade.

Many market watchers expect Italy to be offered some sort of compromise deal, whereby it would be promised EMU membership at a pre-determined later date. Right now, such a deal would be anathema to image-conscious Rome.

"The idea of delaying EMU entrance is not acceptable ... It would have very serious effects on the government's capability to control the economy," said Franco Pavoncello, a professor of politics at Rome's John Cabot universtiy.
The only kind of delay any Italian minister has officially hinted at is one in the selection of initial EMU entrants, which is due to take place early next year.
Foreign Minister Lamberto Dini said on Saturday that the European Union might decide to do this "a bit" later.
This would allow Italy to use 1998 data to back its EMU bid.
"This would be positive for Italy ... the fall in interest rates over the past year will only really start to bear fruit in 1998," said Claudio Tosato, an economist with Deutsche Bank.
But Italy cannot bank on a delay to the decision-making and will have to make sure its 1997 accounts are up to scratch.
Refoundation said last month it would reject fresh taxes or cuts in welfare spending in the forthcoming mini-budget, which will be unveiled before the end of April.
Prodi in turn has said he wants a budget based largely on structural measures, which will have a lasting effect.
Commentators expect a compromise, with the government likely to hack back at some pension handouts, while resorting to one-off measures such as tax amnesties.
In addition, Refoundation wants a budget worth less than 10 trillion lire but on this analysts see no room for compromise.
"After all the efforts this government has made, they're not going to risk everything just for five or six trillion lire," Tosato said. ($ = 1694 Italian Lire)
